nameStory: This little plant gets its "pennywort" name from its round, coin-shaped leaves that look just like tiny green pennies scattered across the ground. The "Sibthorp's" part honors John Sibthorp, an 18th-century English botanist who studied Mediterranean plants, though this particular species actually hails from Southeast Asia.
description: Sibthorp's Pennywort is a tiny creeping plant that forms low mats along the ground, rarely growing more than an inch or two tall. Its most distinctive feature is its collection of small, perfectly round leaves that look like miniature lily pads or coins. This Asian native is slowly spreading in the United States and can pop up in surprisingly diverse places, from lawns to wetland edges. Despite its delicate appearance, it's quite adaptable once it gets established.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Perfectly round, coin-sized leaves that feel smooth and slightly thick, like tiny green lily pads attached to thin stems at the center of each leaf

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that hug the ground, with individual plants rarely exceeding 2 inches in height

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thin, delicate stems that creep along the ground and root at nodes, feeling soft and easily breakable when handled

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous white or greenish flowers in small clusters, so small they're easily overlooked without close inspection

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Leaves have a smooth, waxy feel with slightly thickened texture, and the whole plant feels tender and succulent-like

habitat: This adaptable plant can turn up in a variety of moist locations across New England, from lawn edges and garden borders to pond margins and wetland areas. It prefers consistently moist soil and partial shade, often appearing in areas that stay damp year-round. Look for it creeping along the edges of streams, around water features, or in low-lying areas of yards and parks.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as tiny round leaves begin spreading outward from established patches, with the plant actively growing and expanding its mat-like coverage.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with the most visible leaf development and tiny flowers appearing, though the flowers are so small they're easily missed.
seasonality.fall: Growth slows but leaves typically remain green and visible, continuing to photosynthesize in milder weather.
seasonality.winter: In protected locations, some leaves may persist through mild winters, though the plant generally dies back to underground parts in harsh conditions.

funFact: This tiny plant is popular in the aquarium hobby where it's grown underwater as an aquatic plant, completely submerged, yet it's equally happy creeping across dry land - making it one of the few plants that can thrive both as a terrestrial ground cover and as a fully aquatic species!
confusionNotes: The perfectly round, coin-like leaves make this species quite distinctive, but it might be confused with other small creeping plants in lawns. The key difference is that penny-shaped leaves attached at the center (like tiny umbrellas) - most other small lawn plants have oval or elongated leaves attached at the base.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name connecting it to Sibthorp (who studied Mediterranean plants), this species is actually native to Southeast Asia and is considered an introduced species in New England. It's part of the ivy family, not closely related to the carrot family where many similar-looking plants belong.
compareHints: Unlike American Water-pennywort which has kidney-shaped or lobed leaves, Sibthorp's Pennywort has perfectly round, unlobed leaves. While other pennyworts in the genus typically grow in or near water with larger leaves, Sibthorp's is much smaller overall and more terrestrial, often appearing in regular garden settings rather than strictly aquatic habitats.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American water-pennywort can be distinguished from its relatives by its consistently round leaves and preference for the northeastern climate.
Among New England's water pennyworts, manyflower marshpennywort has the most perfectly circular leaves and the most obvious umbrella-shaped flower clusters.
Among New England's pennyworts, whorled pennywort is the easiest to identify because of its perfectly circular leaves attached at the center.
Unlike its pennywort relatives in New England, floating marsh pennywort is the only one that forms true floating mats on open water.
**[UNCERTAIN]** Compared to its more common cousin American Water-pennywort, this species likely differs in leaf size, flower arrangement, or specific habitat requirements.
